verses.text: David fled from Naioth in Ramah, and came and said before Jonathan, “What have I done? What is my iniquity? What is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?”
He said to him, “Far from it; you will not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small, but that he discloses it to me. Why would my father hide this thing from me? It is not so.”

David swore moreover, and said, “Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes; and he says, ‘Don’t let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved:’ but truly as Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death.”
Then Jonathan said to David, “Whatever your soul desires, I will even do it for you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to dine with the king; but let me go, that I may hide myself in the field to the third day at evening.
If your father misses me at all, then say, ‘David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city; for it is the yearly sacrifice there for all the family.’
If he says, ‘It is well;’ your servant shall have peace: but if he is angry, then know that evil is determined by him.

Therefore deal kindly with your servant; for you have brought your servant into a covenant of Yahweh with you; but if there is iniquity in me, kill me yourself; for why should you bring me to your father?”
Jonathan said, “Far be it from you; for if I should at all know that evil were determined by my father to come on you, then wouldn’t I tell you that?”
Then David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if perchance your father answers you roughly?”
Jonathan said to David, “Come, and let us go out into the field.” They both went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, “By Yahweh, the God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if there is good toward David, won’t I then send to you, and disclose it to you?

Yahweh do so to Jonathan, and more also, should it please my father to do you evil, if I don’t disclose it to you, and send you away, that you may go in peace. May Yahweh be with you, as he has been with my father.
You shall not only while yet I live show me the loving kindness of Yahweh, that I not die;
but you shall also not cut off your kindness from my house forever; no, not when Yahweh has cut off every one of the enemies of David from the surface of the earth.”
So Jonathan made a covenant with David’s house, saying, “Yahweh will require it at the hand of David’s enemies.”
Jonathan caused David to swear again, for the love that he had to him; for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
Then Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
When you have stayed three days, go down quickly, and come to the place where you hid yourself when this started, and remain by the stone Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows on its side, as though I shot at a mark.

Behold, I will send the boy, saying, ‘Go, find the arrows!’ If I tell the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are on this side of you. Take them;’ then come; for there is peace to you and no danger, as Yahweh lives.
But if I say this to the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are beyond you;’ then go your way; for Yahweh has sent you away.
Concerning the matter which you and I have spoken of, behold, Yahweh is between you and me forever.”
So David hid himself in the field. When the new moon had come, the king sat himself down to eat food.
The king sat on his seat, as at other times, even on the seat by the wall; and Jonathan stood up, and Abner sat by Saul’s side, but David’s place was empty.
Nevertheless Saul didn’t say anything that day, for he thought, “Something has happened to him. He is not clean. Surely he is not clean.”
On the next day after the new moon, the second day, David’s place was empty. Saul said to Jonathan his son, “Why doesn’t the son of Jesse come to eat, either yesterday, or today?”
Jonathan answered Saul, “David earnestly asked permission of me to go to Bethlehem.

He said, ‘Please let me go, for our family has a sacrifice in the city. My brother has commanded me to be there. Now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go away and see my brothers.’ Therefore he has not come to the king’s table.”

Then Saul’s anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of a perverse rebellious woman, don’t I know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, you will not be established, nor will your kingdom. Therefore now send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die!”
Jonathan answered Saul his father, and said to him, “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?”
Saul cast his spear at him to strike him. By this Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.
So Jonathan arose from the table in fierce anger, and ate no food the second day of the month; for he was grieved for David, because his father had treated him shamefully.
In the morning, Jonathan went out into the field at the time appointed with David, and a little boy with him.
He said to his boy, “Run, find now the arrows which I shoot.” As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy had come to the place of the arrow which Jonathan had shot, Jonathan cried after the boy, and said, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?”
Jonathan cried after the boy, “Go fast! Hurry! Don’t delay!” Jonathan’s boy gathered up the arrows, and came to his master.
But the boy didn’t know anything. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy, and said to him, “Go, carry them to the city.”

As soon as the boy was gone, David arose out of the south, and fell on his face to the ground, and bowed himself three times. They kissed one another, and wept one with another, and David wept the most.

Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace, because we have both sworn in Yahweh’s name, saying, ‘Yahweh is between me and you, and between my offspring  and your offspring,  forever.’” He arose and departed; and Jonathan went into the city.

footnotes.content: David comes to his truest friend in fear and confusion—"What have I done?" he asks, knowing Saul seeks his life but uncertain of his own fault. This is how we come to Jesus too, sometimes without understanding our true need, just knowing we're in trouble and need help.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan speaks with such easy confidence: "Far from it; you will not die." A true friend doesn't join your fear—he brings you toward the light. Jonathan's loyalty will prove deeper than David's dread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David swears by the Lord and his own life: "there is but a step between me and death." When someone loves you enough to speak plainly about their peril, you know they're not exaggerating—they're asking you to believe the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan's answer is immediate and open: "Whatever your soul desires, I will even do it for you." Real friendship doesn't require proof or lengthy talk—it moves toward the other's need at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asks to skip the new moon feast—a sacred family meal in Israel's calendar. He'll hide three days while Jonathan tests whether Saul's rage is truly aimed at him. Notice David doesn't flee without counsel; he acts with a friend's wisdom and the Lord's providence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David gives Jonathan words to use: "the yearly sacrifice there for all the family" in Bethlehem. A cover story, yes—but one rooted in real custom. Sometimes wisdom means using the plain truth of our circumstances as our shield.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If he is angry, then know that evil is determined by him." David speaks carefully: testing the waters before putting his life in Saul's hands again. Prudence is not faithlessness—it's taking seriously both God and the human heart we're dealing with.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asks Jonathan to "deal kindly" with him and reminds him of their covenant with the Lord. Then—most tenderly—he says, "or kill me yourself; for why should you bring me to your father?" A man choosing trust over fear, putting his life in his friend's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan says "Far be it from you"—rejecting the thought. His love is not fragile; it will not betray David even if Saul commands it. This is how Christ loves us: not dependent on our worthiness, but sovereign and unchanging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who will tell me if perchance your father answers you roughly?" David presses further—not doubting Jonathan, but needing to know how he'll know. In crisis, we need not just loyalty but also a signal, a way to read what's coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Come, and let us go out into the field." Jonathan moves them away from the palace, from Saul's ears, to a place where they can speak freely. Sometimes the Lord leads us to quiet places to remind us of truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan swears "By Yahweh, the God of Israel" and lays out his plan: he'll sound out Saul by tomorrow or the third day and send word to David. A friend's promise is only as good as the God he swears by.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan invokes the harshest covenant oath: "Yahweh do so to Jonathan, and more also," binding himself in the Lord's sight. Then he adds the gentlest wish: "May Yahweh be with you, as he has been with my father." Love always ends in blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You shall not only while yet I live show me the loving kindness of Yahweh, that I not die." Jonathan looks ahead to his own mortality and asks David to remember him—to show him mercy in the day when he cannot return it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "but you shall also not cut off your kindness from my house forever." Jonathan binds David to his family, not just to himself. He trusts that a loyal friend will outlast the friendship and honor the bond even after death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "So Jonathan made a covenant with David's house, saying, 'Yahweh will require it at the hand of David's enemies.'" Covenants in Israel are witnessed by God Himself—He becomes the enforcer of the promise. What humans seal before the Lord, He upholds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Jonathan caused David to swear again, for the love that he had to him; for he loved him as he loved his own soul." This is the heart of it: Jonathan loves David as himself—not less, not conditionally. Such friendships are rare and show us something of Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty." Jonathan knows that absence is the signal—not a word spoken, but a place left vacant. Sometimes what we don't do speaks louder than what we say.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "remain by the stone Ezel"—a specific landmark the two of them know. Even in danger, they have a place marked out, a stone between them. The Lord often gives us such markers in our seasons of hiding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will shoot three arrows on its side, as though I shot at a mark." Jonathan's signal is disguised—a young man shooting at targets looks innocent to any watcher. Wisdom sometimes means hiding truth in plain sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If Jonathan calls to the boy, "The arrows are on this side of you," then David is safe and can come near. If danger passes and there's peace, the Lord makes it known. We learn to read the small signs of His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the call is "The arrows are beyond you," then David must flee at once—"Yahweh has sent you away." Jonathan speaks of the Lord's sending, not his own decision. He knows his friend's escape is in God's hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Concerning the matter which you and I have spoken of, behold, Yahweh is between you and me forever." This is covenant language—the Lord Himself stands as witness and guardian of what they've sworn. A bond sealed before Him cannot be broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "David hid himself in the field. When the new moon had come, the king sat himself down to eat food." The test begins: Saul feasts while David, innocent, lies hidden. Sometimes the righteous are cast down while the proud sit at the table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "David's place was empty." One absent seat—and everything that follows flows from it. In a king's court, an empty chair means missing rank, missing loyalty, missing explanation. The silence of absence speaks volumes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul says nothing that first day, assuming David is unclean—maybe ritually unfit. Ignorance can sometimes be merciful; it holds back the hand that would strike. But it doesn't last long.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "On the next day after the new moon, the second day, David's place was empty." Now Saul notices—and questions Jonathan directly. The truth cannot hide forever; the king's suspicion is aroused.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan uses the exact lie they prepared: David asked permission to go to Bethlehem. A friend's lie in defense of the innocent is still sin—yet Jonathan speaks, and the burden falls on him, not David.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan speaks more: "family sacrifice," "my brother commanded," "if I have found favor...let me go." He embellishes skillfully, grounding the lie in family obligation and respect. But Saul is no longer fooled—his rage is kindling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul's anger breaks: "You son of a perverse rebellious woman!" A king's curse is not mere words—it's a judgment spoken from a throne. When Saul turns on Jonathan, his cruelty shows its true depth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, you will not be established, nor will your kingdom. Therefore now send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die!" Saul sees David as a rival for the throne and demands Jonathan betray him. Love and loyalty are put to the test.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan asks simply: "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?" The question of justice—unanswerable. David has done nothing but be beloved and faithful, yet Saul wants his death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Saul cast his spear at him." The king tries to murder his own son over a question. In that moment, Jonathan knows with certainty: his father is bent on David's death, and no word of his will change it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan leaves the table "in fierce anger" and fasts—grieved for David, ashamed of his father. He chooses his friend's pain over the king's favor. This is when family loyalty cracks open to show where the true allegiance lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In the morning, Jonathan went out into the field at the time appointed with David." Despite everything—the spear, the curse, the broken table—Jonathan keeps his covenant word. He shows up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan tells the boy to fetch the arrows, then shoots one beyond him. Each arrow is a truth wrapped in seeming play—the signal David needs, disguised as sport.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Isn't the arrow beyond you?" Jonathan shouts—the terrible word David has been dreading to hear. Beyond means danger, means flee, means Saul is coming for his blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Go fast! Hurry! Don't delay!" Jonathan urges the boy—his words urgent with love and the weight of what he's about to lose. The boy gathers the arrows, unaware he's watching a friendship break apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The boy didn't know anything. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter." Some truths are too deep for the innocent to carry. Only those who love bear the knowledge and the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan gives his weapons to the boy and sends him back to the city. He's sending away the only person who can prove he was there—erasing his own alibi to protect David's secret.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David rises and "fell on his face to the ground, and bowed himself three times. They kissed one another, and wept one with another, and David wept the most." When two souls know their time together is ending, the silence of embrace speaks louder than any vow. Readers today still hear an echo of this grief—the ache when love and duty must part.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Go in peace, because we have both sworn in Yahweh's name... Yahweh is between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever." Jonathan's last words bind their promise not just to themselves but to generations—David will remember, and so will Israel. They part, but the covenant remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
